author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: Locked Up and Criminalized: People on the Move Face a Broken System on Crete’s Shores
content:
Crete, Greece — People on the move arriving on Crete are held in makeshift facilities where they have no rights, as authorities freeze asylum registration while implementing the EU’s contested new Migration and Asylum Pact.

The abandoned Kitrenosis industrial complex sits along the highway connecting the cities of Rethymno and Heraklion, on Crete’s northern coast. The warehouses, disused for years, look out over a cliff that drops straight into the sea. Scattered across the outdoor lot are piles of objects hinting at a transient human presence: faded clothing, broken chargers, crumpled cigarette packs.

Crete has no dedicated reception system, and Kitrenosis is one of the stopgap solutions authorities have turned to after transferring people from the island’s southern shores, where boats arrive, to temporary holding sites in the north.

According to local media reports, the site was last used in December 2025, when it held more than 500 people. It has sat empty since, but inside one of the warehouses, traces of makeshift shelter remain. The space has no windows — a beam of sunlight creeping in through the gap in a broken gate is the only light inside the facility. The floor is littered with the remains of packaged food, half-empty water bottles, gym mats and flattened cardboard boxes.

author: By Phil Mandelbaum, Contributor
title: Reporting from Gaza with Palestinian Poet Ahmed Sarsour
content:
“It’s not just about what’s happening in Palestine, it’s happening everywhere. The same forces that are controlling the world, the capitalist and imperialist forces, they are the ones who started the war in Sudan, and they are the ones waging wars in communities in every country in the world, like in Congo and Turtle Island, and Cuba and Venezuela,” Ahmed Sarsour tells me.

It’s the afternoon of Friday, June 26, and Sarsour is struggling to stay on the call amid interruptions in electricity. The 33-year-old Palestinian poet is speaking to Unicorn Riot from his birthplace, his grandparents’ home in the center of Gaza in the city of Deir Al-Balah. Shaken but still standing after three separate bombings, the house sits adjacent to rubble from their neighbors’ former home. The local mosque has also been destroyed.

“The Internet is not stable, there’s just a local vendor here in the Gaza Strip — and we are dependent on it because there hasn’t been electricity in Gaza since the seventh of October,” Sarsour says.

On October 7, 2023, Israel declared war, launching an attack on Gaza that has left the majority of Gaza’s 2.3 million people displaced. According to the official numbers reported nearly 75,000 Palestinians have been killed while researchers find the total could be fifty percent higher with a death toll surpassing 100,000 .

author: By Dingane Xaba, Unicorn Riot
title: Minneapolis Unions & Activists Honor 92nd Anniversary of 1934 Truckers Strike
content:
Minneapolis, MN — On July 19, labor activists and organizers held an annual memorial commemorating workers who died during the Minneapolis truckers strike of 1934. It marked the 92nd anniversary of “Bloody Friday” in which two unarmed strikers were killed and 67 others shot after local police opened fire on demonstrators at the intersection of North 7th Street and 3rd Avenue in downtown Minneapolis.

Four days later over 100,000 people flooded the streets during the funeral procession of the two slain workers, Henry Ness and John Belor. This quickly became a rallying cry not just for local truck drivers but for a burgeoning national labor movement demanding better pay and improved safety conditions across the board.

Increased pressure from a strong local and national union movement forced Minnesota’s business owners — then represented by the notorious anti-union Citizens Alliance — to concede to the strikers demands. It was a huge victory not only for Minnesota unions but for the entire national labor movement leading to overall improved working conditions and enshrining the legal right for workers to organize on the job floor.

Despite record breaking heat, and simultaneous competing events in the World Cup final and the Minneapolis Aquatennial, dozens of people came to the event to pay their respects.

author: By Aris Dimitrakopoulos, Contributor
title: As Senegal Cracks Down on LGBTQ Rights, Activists Seek Help From Abroad
content:
“I prefer to remain anonymous because of the authorities in Senegal,” Mamadou, one of the founders of the Senegalese LGBTQ rights organization Free Senegal, told Unicorn Riot. Speaking under an alias, Mamadou agreed to speak with Unicorn Riot only if he could remain anonymous. He fled the country in 2021 after years of harassment and is one of many now worried for their safety amid a wave of anti-LGBTQ repression that took hold this year.




His fears are not unfounded. Since February, Senegalese authorities have initiated a crackdown against the LGBTQ community, reportedly arresting hundreds across the country. Local newspapers announce new arrests every week, including of celebrities.




The recent crackdown started after the dismantling of a suspected French-Senegalese pedophilia ring in early February. It culminated with Parliament passing a new anti-LGBTQ law by an overwhelming majority in March, which doubled prison sentences for “acts against nature” to up to 10 years.




Under this provision, the law equates same-sex relationships with sexual crimes such as bestiality and necrophilia. Furthermore, in a separate article, it stipulates a sentence of up to seven years in prison for the “promotion or financing” of homosexuality, bisexuality, or transgender identity.

author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: Inside Greece’s Refugee Camps, Gender-Based Violence Is Built Into the System
content:
Ritsona, Greece — Since 2022, the German collective Rosa Rolling Safespace has been providing a mobile safe space for women living in refugee camps around Athens. Their work shows that gender-based violence in these settings is not incidental but structural, a direct product of European and Greek migration policies.




Ritsona is a small town about 47 miles north of Athens. Driving through the surrounding countryside, it is hard to miss a sprawling cluster of gray containers encircled by barbed wire, surveillance cameras, and heavy metal gates monitored by police. It is one of the largest refugee camps in mainland Greece — according to 

the latest data

 released by the Greek Ministry of Migration and Asylum, it has a nominal capacity of nearly 3,000 people.




Around the camp, hills and wind turbines stretch as far as the eye can see, occasionally interrupted by some industrial facilities breaking the monotony of the empty countryside. Once a week, however, a small dusty lot a few hundred meters from the camp’s main entrance comes to life.







Rosa Rolling Safespace setting up outside Ritsona camp. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.







It is a Wednesday, and around midday two white vans appear at the far end of the long road running alongside the Ritsona camp. They park in the lot, and a group of about ten volunteers immediately get to work setting up a safe space

author: By Sophia Potsi, Contributor
title: In Athens, Albania’s Diaspora Watches a Revolt at Home, and Finds Its Own Voice
content:
People have taken to the streets in Albania for over a month now. What started as a protest about environmental concerns and a luxury resort tied to President Trump’s son-in-law has turned into a mass movement against the government, with people demanding the resignation of the Prime Minister Edi Rama.




The story begins with a development plan for the Vjosa-Narta lagoon, a protected wetland on Albania’s Adriatic coast, and the nearby uninhabited island of 

Sazan

, once a secret Soviet-era military base, now eyed as the site of a luxury tourism complex. The project is reportedly worth well over one billion euros and is tied to Affinity Partners, the investment firm through which American businessman and politician Jared Kushner is acquiring Sazan. The firm was established to use Saudi Arabian capital to facilitate investments between Israel and the Arab world.




Kushner and his wife Ivanka Trump have spoken publicly about their vision for the area; high-end, eco-luxury, a yacht marina, wellness spa, and fine-dining restaurants, transforming a stretch of pristine coastline into a five-star destination.




For the Albanian government, this was framed as a historic opportunity, a flagship investment that would put the country on the map as a premier Mediterranean destination and bring much-needed foreign capital into a struggling economy.
